```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.8, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

A categorical sequence records which state a unit occupies at each of many
ordered time points: the rating a participant gives at each prompt of an
experience sampling study, the activity a student performs at each step of a
session, the role a person holds in each month of a career. Drawn on a single
horizontal axis, a sequence of more than a few dozen positions either becomes
too narrow to read or too wide to fit on a page. A snake plot folds the axis
into horizontal bands joined by U-turn arcs, so a long sequence keeps its
order and every position keeps a readable width.

This guide covers the three functions for categorical sequences.
`sequence_snake()` draws one sequence position by position, as coloured
blocks or as a thin rug. `timeline_snake()` draws a small number of long
phases from a table of start and end dates. `multi_snake()` draws many
sequences at once, either one tick per sequence (index mode) or the share of
sequences in each state at each time point (distribution mode). Continuous
and clock-time data are covered in [the activity guide](activity.html);
colours and reading order in
[the palettes and layout guide](palettes-and-layout.html).

```{r package}
library(snakeplot)
```

## Data

The examples use `ema_beeps`, the beep-level records of an experience sampling
study in which 321 university students rated their emotions on prompts
("beeps") sent to their phones over 14 study days (Neubauer & Schmiedek,
2024; data CC-BY 4.0 at <https://osf.io/bhq3p>). Each row is one answered
beep.

- **Participant:** `id` — anonymised identifier.
- **Study day:** `day` — 1 to 14.
- **Time stamp:** `start_time` — date and clock time of the beep (POSIXct).
- **Ratings:** `happy`, `angry` — self-reported happiness and anger on a
  1–5 scale (rescaled from the original 1–7).

```{r data}
head(ema_beeps)
with(ema_beeps, c(beeps = length(id), participants = length(unique(id)),
                  days = length(unique(day))))
```

The data hold 11,474 answered beeps from 321 participants over 14 study days.
The ratings are integers; the examples below give them verbal labels so that
the legends read as a response scale.

## One participant's ratings as a sequence

The first question concerns a single participant: in what order did
participant `xcVDLRQOwn` report each level of happiness, beep after beep? The
ratings are converted to a factor with labelled levels, and the counts per
level and the number of changes between consecutive beeps are computed.

```{r one-participant}
scale_labels <- c("Not at all", "Slightly", "Moderately", "Quite", "Extremely")
mood <- transform(subset(ema_beeps, id == "xcVDLRQOwn"),
                  happiness = factor(happy, levels = 1:5, labels = scale_labels))
nrow(mood)
with(mood, table(happiness))
with(mood, sum(head(happiness, -1) != tail(happiness, -1)))
```

The participant answered 69 beeps. The most frequent rating is *Quite*
(32 beeps), followed by *Slightly* (22), *Moderately* (10) and *Extremely*
(5); *Not at all* never occurs. The
rating changes between 47 of the 68 pairs of consecutive beeps, so the
sequence is dominated by short runs rather than long stable spells.

`sequence_snake()` takes the sequence as a vector, a comma-separated string,
or a data frame whose first character or factor column holds the states.
Without `states`, the states are taken in order of first appearance, not
from the factor levels; passing `states` fixes the legend order to the order
of the scale, and a five-colour palette gives one colour per level.

```{r sequence-block}
sequence_snake(subset(mood, select = happiness),
               states = scale_labels,
               colors = snake_palette("sunset", n = 5))
```

Each block is one beep, coloured by its rating, in the order in which the
beeps were answered. The blocks continue through the U-turn arcs, so no
position is skipped where one band ends and the next begins; the label above
each band gives the range of beep numbers it holds. Because 47 of 68
consecutive pairs differ, most blocks have a neighbour of a different colour,
which is the visual counterpart of the frequent changes computed above.

## Block and rug styles

The block style fills the full band height and suits sequences of up to a few
hundred positions. The rug style draws each position as a thin coloured
mark on a light band, which keeps individual positions apart when the
sequence is long or when the eye should follow the positions rather than the
runs.

```{r sequence-rug}
sequence_snake(subset(mood, select = happiness),
               states = scale_labels,
               colors = snake_palette("sunset", n = 5),
               style = "rug")
```

The encoding is the same as in the block version: one mark per beep, in beep
order, coloured by the rating. The rug style also accepts `jitter`, a
vertical scatter of the marks; it is off by default because a scattered rug
reads as a distribution rather than as an ordered sequence.

## Reading direction

`sequence_snake()` reads every band from left to right by default
(`flow = "natural"`), like lines of text. With `flow = "snake"` the direction
alternates, so the sequence runs left to right in the first band, right to
left in the second, and so on, and consecutive positions on either side of a
U-turn sit next to each other.

```{r sequence-snake-flow}
sequence_snake(subset(mood, select = happiness),
               states = scale_labels,
               colors = snake_palette("sunset", n = 5),
               flow = "snake")
```

The natural flow is the better default when readers compare the same
position across bands; the alternating flow keeps the path continuous at the
turns. [The palettes and layout guide](palettes-and-layout.html) shows how
the reading direction of every band can be checked from the returned layout.

## Phases with dates

A career, a degree or a project consists of a few long phases, each with a
start and an end date. The question here is how the time of a doctoral
project is divided among its phases. The phases are entered as a small table,
and the length of each phase in months is computed from its dates.

```{r phd-table}
phd <- data.frame(
  phase = c("Coursework", "Literature review", "Data collection",
            "Analysis", "Writing", "Defence"),
  start = as.Date(c("2019-09-01", "2020-06-01", "2021-03-01",
                    "2022-05-01", "2023-02-01", "2024-01-01")),
  end   = as.Date(c("2020-05-01", "2021-02-01", "2022-04-01",
                    "2023-01-01", "2023-12-01", "2024-03-01"))
)
phd_months <- transform(phd, months = 12 * (as.integer(format(end, "%Y")) -
                                            as.integer(format(start, "%Y"))) +
                                      as.integer(format(end, "%m")) -
                                      as.integer(format(start, "%m")) + 1)
phd_months
with(phd_months, sum(months))
```

The project spans 55 months. Data collection is the longest phase (14
months), writing takes 11, coursework, the literature review and the analysis
take 9 each, and the defence 3.

`timeline_snake()` takes the three columns (state, start, end), expands them
into one block per month, writes each phase name inside its run, and labels
the month at which each phase ends.

```{r timeline, fig.height = 4.2}
timeline_snake(phd,
               colors = c("#E69F00", "#56B4E9", "#009E73",
                          "#CC79A7", "#0072B2", "#D55E00"))
```

Each band holds about 20 months, so the 55 months fold into three bands. The
width of a phase is proportional to its length in months, which places the
14-month data collection and the 3-month defence on the same scale. The
transition labels mark the last month of each phase; the band labels give
the year.

## Many sequences at once

The last question concerns the whole cohort rather than one participant:
how many beeps did each participant answer on each study day, and how does
that change over the 14 days? The number of answered beeps per participant
and day is a categorical state from 0 (no beep answered) to 5 (all beeps
answered). The first table holds one row per participant-day; the second
gives, for each day, the percentage of the 321 participants in each state.

```{r answered}
daily <- as.data.frame(xtabs(~ id + day, data = ema_beeps),
                       responseName = "beeps")
head(daily)
round(100 * prop.table(xtabs(~ day + beeps, data = daily), margin = 1))
```

On day 1, 37% of the participants answered all five beeps and 5% answered
none. By day 14, the share answering none has risen to 45% and the share
answering all five has fallen to 10%. The decline is not uniform: from day 7
to day 8 the share answering all five rises from 14% to 21% and the share
answering none falls from 27% to 25%, before the decline resumes. Answering
falls off over the study, with a partial recovery at the start of the second
week.

`multi_snake()` takes a matrix or data frame with one row per sequence and
one column per time point. The cross-tabulation of participants by day gives
that layout directly.

```{r multi-distribution, fig.height = 4.6}
answered <- as.data.frame.matrix(xtabs(~ id + day, data = ema_beeps))
multi_snake(answered, type = "distribution",
            states = as.character(0:5),
            colors = snake_palette("blues", n = 6),
            rows = 5)
```

In distribution mode each block is one study day, drawn as a stacked bar of
the percentages in the table above, from 0 beeps (lightest) to 5 beeps
(darkest). The row labels give the days each band holds. In version 0.3.3
`multi_snake()` assigns the time points that fall on a U-turn to the arc but
fills the arc in neutral grey, so the days between two consecutive row
labels are counted in the layout but not drawn; the table above remains the
complete record.

Index mode keeps the individual sequences: each block contains one thin tick
per participant, coloured by that participant's state on that day.
`sort_by = "freq"` orders the participants by their most frequent state, so
participants with similar answering patterns sit next to each other in every
block.

```{r multi-index, fig.height = 4.6}
multi_snake(answered, type = "index",
            states = as.character(0:5),
            colors = snake_palette("blues", n = 6),
            rows = 5, sort_by = "freq")
```

Distribution mode answers how many participants are in each state on each
day; index mode answers whether the same participants stay in the same state
across days.

## When to use which

- `sequence_snake()` — one long categorical sequence, one position per
  block; block style for runs, rug style for many positions.
- `timeline_snake()` — a few long phases given as start and end dates;
  phase names and transition months are written on the plot.
- `multi_snake(type = "distribution")` — many sequences summarised as the
  share in each state at each time point.
- `multi_snake(type = "index")` — many sequences drawn individually, sorted
  so that similar sequences are adjacent.

For ordinal ratings that should be read as distributions per day rather than
as sequences, `survey_snake()` with `var` and `day` is the better tool; see
[the daily emotions case study](case-daily-emotions.html).

## Reference

Neubauer, A. B., & Schmiedek, F. (2024). Approaching academic adjustment on
multiple time scales. *Zeitschrift für Erziehungswissenschaft, 27*(1),
147–168. <https://doi.org/10.1007/s11618-023-01182-8>
